questions.question:
An AWS account has 150 IAM users spread across three departments. The security team must enforce MFA for all console logins. Users who have not yet enrolled an MFA device must still be able to configure their own MFA before gaining access to other AWS services. Enforcement must apply automatically to all current and future IAM users without per-user intervention.

Which IAM configuration enforces this requirement with the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Create an IAM group for all users and attach a policy that denies all actions except `iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice`, `iam:EnableMFADevice`, `iam:GetUser`, `iam:ListMFADevices`, `iam:ResyncMFADevice`, and `sts:GetSessionToken` using a `BoolIfExists` condition on `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: false`. Automate group membership for new users via an account provisioning process.
choices.explanation: The deny-with-exceptions pattern is the correct enforcement mechanism. A `Deny` with `NotAction` blocks all API calls when MFA is absent while the exempted actions let users self-enroll an MFA device. `BoolIfExists` handles sessions where the key may not be present (e.g., CLI without a session token), preventing unintended lockouts.

choices.text: Apply an SCP at the root OU level that denies all API calls when `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is `false`, targeting only member account IAM users through a condition on `aws:PrincipalType: IAMUser`.
choices.explanation: SCPs apply to all principals in the OU and cannot be reliably scoped to IAM users alone via `aws:PrincipalType` for console enforcement. More critically, this approach omits the self-enrollment exception list, locking users out before they can configure MFA.

choices.text: Enable the AWS Config managed rule `mfa-enabled-for-iam-console-access` with an automatic remediation action that suspends console access for non-compliant users until MFA is manually verified by an administrator.
choices.explanation: AWS Config is a detective control that evaluates resource configuration asynchronously. It cannot enforce in-session MFA requirements in real time, block console access proactively, or provide a self-enrollment window. Remediation actions also introduce manual toil at scale.

choices.text: Configure AWS IAM Identity Center to require MFA at the application level for all permission sets, relying on Identity Center's built-in MFA enforcement to replace direct IAM user console policies.
choices.explanation: IAM Identity Center MFA governs SSO-federated sessions only. It has no effect on IAM user console logins, which authenticate independently through the AWS Management Console sign-in page. Users with both IAM credentials and SSO access could still sign in without MFA via the IAM user path.

questions.tip: Consider which IAM policy element can simultaneously block broad access and preserve a narrow set of self-service actions based on session context.
questions.explanation:
The IAM deny-with-exceptions pattern is the AWS-recommended approach for enforcing MFA enrollment. A policy using `Effect: Deny` with `NotAction` activates when `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is `false`, blocking all actions except a curated self-service list that lets users register their MFA device. Attaching this to an IAM group scales automatically as users are added.

**Why it works:** `BoolIfExists` handles both authenticated console sessions and CLI/SDK calls where the key may be absent, preventing unintended lockouts for service roles. The exempted actions cover the full MFA device registration flow.

**Why the others fail:**
- SCP at root OU: Cannot be scoped to IAM users alone; omits the self-enrollment exception, locking users out before they can enroll.
- AWS Config remediation: Evaluates configuration asynchronously; cannot intercept or block API calls in real time.
- IAM Identity Center MFA: Applies only to SSO-federated sessions; direct IAM user console logins follow a separate authentication path.

**Implementation:** Console > IAM > User Groups > Create group > Attach inline or managed deny policy with `BoolIfExists` condition. Automate group membership through your provisioning pipeline.

questions.question:
Thirty member accounts exist under a management account in AWS Organizations. Root user credentials for member accounts must be prevented from signing in under any circumstances. Any future accounts joined to the organization must automatically inherit the same protection, with minimal per-account configuration.

Which approach provides the strongest protection against root user access in member accounts with automatic enforcement for new accounts?

choices.text: Enable centralized root access management in AWS Organizations on the management account, which removes root user sign-in capability from all current and future member accounts while preserving the management account root for break-glass use.
choices.explanation: Centralized root access management deactivates root credentials at the member account level organization-wide. New accounts created in the organization automatically inherit this protection, satisfying both the minimal-configuration and future-proof requirements.

choices.text: Apply an SCP to the root OU that denies all actions for the root user using the condition `aws:PrincipalType: Root`, and exclude the management account via a target exclusion to prevent lockout.
choices.explanation: SCPs restrict what the root user can do after authentication but cannot prevent root console sign-in itself. Root credentials remain active, and an attacker who obtains root credentials can still authenticate; only subsequent API calls would be blocked.

choices.text: Reset the root user password for every member account to a long random string stored in AWS Secrets Manager in the management account, and delete any existing root access keys to remove programmatic access.
choices.explanation: Storing a randomly generated root password in Secrets Manager reduces practical risk but does not deactivate root credentials. An attacker who compromises the management account or Secrets Manager could retrieve the stored passwords and still sign in as root.

choices.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty across all member accounts with an organization-level detector and configure an EventBridge rule to invoke a Lambda function that changes the root password when a `Policy:IAMUser/RootCredentialUsage` finding fires.
choices.explanation: This is a reactive detective control. GuardDuty can detect root usage and trigger automated remediation, but the response occurs after unauthorized activity has begun. It does not prevent initial root sign-in or provide protection before a finding is generated.

questions.tip: Distinguish between controls that deactivate credentials at the identity layer versus controls that restrict or detect activity after authentication.
questions.explanation:
Centralized root access management in AWS Organizations is correct because it is the only option that removes root sign-in capability at the credential level for member accounts. All other options either restrict post-authentication behavior or respond reactively.

**Why it works:** When enabled on the management account, centralized root access management deactivates the root user password and MFA device for all current member accounts. New accounts created under the organization automatically have root credentials deactivated. The management account root is unaffected, preserving break-glass access.

**Why the others fail:**
- SCP with `aws:PrincipalType: Root`: Blocks root API actions after login but not the login itself; root credentials remain active.
- Random password in Secrets Manager: Reduces practical access but does not deactivate credentials; compromising Secrets Manager restores the attack path.
- GuardDuty + EventBridge + Lambda: Reactive; detection and remediation occur after unauthorized access has started.

**Implementation:** Console > AWS Organizations > Settings > Root access management > Enable centralized root access. The setting propagates automatically to all existing and future member accounts.

choices.text: `iam:GetUser` - retrieving the current user's own details
choices.explanation: `iam:GetUser` appears in the `NotAction` list, which excludes it from the `Deny` statement. When `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is `false`, all actions not in `NotAction` are denied. Because `iam:GetUser` is in the exemption list, it remains permitted.

choices.text: `s3:ListBuckets` - listing all S3 buckets in the account
choices.explanation: `s3:ListBuckets` is not in the `NotAction` list. With `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` evaluated as `false`, the `Deny` statement applies to all actions not exempted. This call would return `AccessDenied`.

choices.text: `ec2:DescribeInstances` - listing EC2 instances across all Regions
choices.explanation: `ec2:DescribeInstances` is not in the `NotAction` list. The deny covers all non-exempted actions when MFA is absent, so this call would return `AccessDenied`.

choices.text: `iam:CreateUser` - creating a new IAM user in the account
choices.explanation: `iam:CreateUser` is not in the `NotAction` list and is therefore subject to the `Deny` when `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is `false`. This action is blocked until the user completes MFA enrollment and re-authenticates with a valid MFA token.

questions.tip: Focus on how `NotAction` interacts with `Effect: Deny` - identify which actions are excluded from the deny statement rather than which are included.
questions.explanation:
The policy uses `Effect: Deny` combined with `NotAction`, which means: deny everything except the listed actions. The `BoolIfExists` condition activates this deny when `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is `false`.

**Why it works:** `iam:GetUser` is in the `NotAction` list, which excludes it from the deny. The user can call `GetUser` to confirm their identity even before MFA setup. All other listed actions support the full MFA device registration flow.

**Why the others fail:**
- `s3:ListBuckets`: Not in `NotAction`; denied when MFA is absent.
- `ec2:DescribeInstances`: Not in `NotAction`; denied when MFA is absent.
- `iam:CreateUser`: Not in `NotAction`; denied when MFA is absent.

**Implementation:** This policy is best attached to an IAM group via Console > IAM > User Groups > Group > Permissions > Add permissions > Create inline policy.

questions.question:
During a security audit of a standalone AWS account that is not part of an organization, a team finds the root user has a valid password, no registered MFA device, and two active access keys. Two independent preventive controls must be implemented to minimize the risk of unauthorized root user access.

Which TWO actions should the team take to reduce the risk of unauthorized root user access?

choices.text: Enable a virtual or hardware MFA device on the root user to require a second authentication factor for all root console sign-ins, storing the MFA seed or device in a physically secured vault.
choices.explanation: Enabling MFA is the highest-impact preventive control for root access. Even if the root password is compromised, an attacker cannot complete root console sign-in without possession of the registered MFA device or seed.

choices.text: Delete both root user access keys to eliminate the programmatic attack surface, since root access keys grant unrestricted API access that cannot be scoped or restricted by any IAM policy.
choices.explanation: Root access keys bypass all IAM permission boundaries and policies. Deleting them removes the programmatic attack path entirely. AWS best practice states that root access keys should never exist; if present, they must be deleted immediately.

choices.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the `ConsoleLogin` CloudTrail event source filtered to root user sign-ins, and notify the security team via SNS whenever root authentication is detected.
choices.explanation: A CloudWatch alarm on root login events is a detective control, not a preventive one. It reduces time-to-detect unauthorized root access but does not prevent it. The question asks for controls that minimize the risk of unauthorized access, which requires preventive measures.

choices.text: Update the root user email address to a non-guessable alias to obscure the login identity and reduce targeted phishing risk against the root account credentials.
choices.explanation: The root user login identity is the account's registered email address. Changing the account email is possible but is not a recognized security control - it does not prevent an attacker who already knows the account ID from attempting root sign-in, and it introduces operational risk if the new address is not carefully managed.

choices.text: Attach an IAM policy to the root user that denies all API calls except account management actions, limiting the blast radius of any unauthorized root session.
choices.explanation: IAM policies, permission boundaries, and SCPs do not apply to the root user of an AWS account. The root user has full, unrestricted access regardless of any attached identity policy. This is a fundamental AWS constraint - root user access cannot be limited by IAM.

questions.tip: Identify which controls act at or before the authentication step versus which controls observe or restrict activity after authentication succeeds.
questions.explanation:
Enabling MFA and deleting root access keys are the two correct preventive controls for a standalone account.

**Why they work:** MFA requires physical possession of a registered device, defeating password-only attacks including credential stuffing and phishing. Deleting access keys eliminates the programmatic attack surface entirely - root keys provide unrestricted API access that bypasses all IAM policies.

**Why the others fail:**
- CloudWatch alarm on root login: Detective control only; it alerts after unauthorized access occurs, not before.
- Changing root email: Not a recognized security control; an attacker with the account ID can still attempt root sign-in regardless of the email address.
- IAM policy on root user: IAM policies do not restrict the root user. Root user access is unconditional and cannot be scoped by any attached identity policy.

**Implementation:** Sign in as root > Console > IAM > Security credentials > Multi-factor authentication > Assign MFA device. For access keys: same page > Access keys > Delete for each key.

questions.question:
An IAM user's long-term access key has been found exposed in a public GitHub repository. The breach must be contained immediately and the IAM user restored to a secure state.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order to remediate the exposed access key.

choices.text: Disable the exposed access key via `aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive` to immediately stop unauthorized use while preserving the key ID for forensic log correlation.
choices.explanation: Disabling the key first stops active unauthorized use immediately. Setting the key to `Inactive` rather than deleting it preserves the key ID, which is needed to correlate CloudTrail events and determine what actions were taken during the exposure window.

choices.text: Review AWS CloudTrail logs filtered by the compromised access key ID to identify all API actions taken and determine the full scope of unauthorized activity.
choices.explanation: After stopping active use, CloudTrail investigation determines what resources were accessed or modified. Performing this step before remediation ensures you know the complete blast radius and do not miss affected resources when cleaning up.

choices.text: Remediate all resources affected during the unauthorized period - for example, rotating database passwords, revoking active IAM role sessions created by the attacker, and removing any unauthorized IAM users or policies.
choices.explanation: After understanding the scope from CloudTrail, remediating affected resources eliminates any backdoors or compromised credentials introduced during the unauthorized period before the user is restored to service.

choices.text: Delete the disabled access key and issue a replacement access key for the IAM user, distributing the new credentials through a secure out-of-band channel.
choices.explanation: Deleting the compromised key and creating a replacement is the final step. It is performed last to ensure forensic investigation is complete and all affected resources are remediated before normal user access is restored.

questions.tip: Consider which step minimizes ongoing risk while preserving the information needed for a complete investigation, then work through the logical dependencies between steps.
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence is: disable the key → investigate via CloudTrail → remediate affected resources → delete and replace the key.

Disabling first stops active unauthorized use without losing the key ID for forensic correlation. CloudTrail investigation precedes remediation because you cannot know what to remediate until you understand the full scope. Remediating affected resources before issuing a new key ensures no backdoors remain active when the user returns to service. Deleting the old key and creating a replacement is the final restoration step.

**Implementation:** `aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE --status Inactive --user-name username` → `aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE` → remediate findings → `aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE --user-name username` + `aws iam create-access-key --user-name username`.

skills: 2.1.1: Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements.
questions.question:
Orders are processed through a central checkout service on AWS. When an order is confirmed, an inventory service, a shipping service, and a fraud detection service must each independently receive and process every order event. The inventory service experiences scheduled maintenance windows lasting up to 10 minutes, during which it cannot consume messages.

Which architecture ensures all three services receive every order event, maintains message delivery during downstream outages, and allows each service to process events at its own rate?

choices.text: Create an Amazon SQS standard queue for order events and configure all three downstream services as consumers using long polling, relying on SQS message visibility timeouts to prevent duplicate processing across services.
choices.explanation: SQS standard queues use a competing consumer model: each message is delivered to exactly one consumer. Once any service reads and deletes a message, the other two services never receive it. This is not fan-out delivery.

choices.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus and configure three rules, each routing order events directly to a target Lambda function representing the inventory, shipping, and fraud services, with Lambda async retry and a dead-letter queue configured on each function.
choices.explanation: EventBridge routing directly to Lambda lacks a durable per-service message buffer. During a 10-minute maintenance window, Lambda invocations will fail and the built-in async retry policy (2 retries over a few minutes) does not retain messages for the full outage duration. A persistent queue is required to absorb extended outages.

choices.text: Create an Amazon SNS topic for order confirmations and subscribe a dedicated Amazon SQS standard queue for each downstream service, allowing each service to poll its own queue independently.
choices.explanation: The SNS fan-out to SQS pattern publishes each order event once to SNS, which delivers it simultaneously to all three subscribed SQS queues. Each queue buffers messages independently, retaining events during the inventory service's maintenance window and allowing each service to consume at its own pace without affecting the others.

choices.text: Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue for order events with a message group ID assigned per downstream service, and configure all three services as consumers so each receives only messages belonging to its own group, preserving strict per-service ordering throughout processing.
choices.explanation: SQS FIFO queues with message group IDs control ordering within a queue for a single consumer type - they do not support multiple independent consumers each receiving the same message. Messages are still consumed competitively, and each order event can reach only one of the three services.

questions.tip: Identify which pattern delivers the same event independently to multiple consumers while providing per-consumer durability that can absorb downstream outages.
questions.explanation:
The SNS + SQS fan-out pattern is the canonical AWS architecture for delivering the same event to multiple independent downstream services. SNS publishes the message once and simultaneously delivers it to all subscribed SQS queues. Each queue acts as an independent, durable buffer.

**Why it works:** SNS guarantees delivery to each subscribed SQS queue. Messages persist in each queue independently - during the inventory service's 10-minute maintenance window, messages accumulate in its queue and are processed automatically when the service recovers, with no message loss and no impact on the shipping or fraud service queues.

**Why the others fail:**
- Shared SQS standard queue with competing consumers: Each SQS message is delivered to exactly one consumer. All three services compete for the same messages, so each order event reaches only one service.
- EventBridge rules directly to Lambda: Lambda async retry covers only short failure windows (2 retries over a few minutes). A 10-minute maintenance window exceeds built-in retry behavior without an SQS buffer to retain messages during the outage.
- SQS FIFO with message group IDs per service: Message group IDs manage ordering within a single queue for one consumer - they do not enable multiple independent consumers to each receive the same message.

**Implementation:** Console > SNS > Create topic > Add subscriptions. `aws sns subscribe --topic-arn <arn> --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint <queue-arn>` repeated for each downstream SQS queue.

skills: 2.1.1: Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements.
questions.question:
During peak live sports events, a streaming platform ingests 160,000 sensor messages per second with strict per-game ordering requirements. Four independent analytics teams must each consume the full message stream simultaneously without sharing read throughput or competing for access to the same records.

Which AWS service and configuration best satisfies the ordering, throughput, and consumer isolation requirements?

choices.text: Amazon SQS FIFO queues with message group IDs mapped to game IDs and four separate queue URLs per analytics team, using 20-second long polling with batch sizes of 10 and SQS redrive policies applied per queue to handle processing failures.
choices.explanation: SQS FIFO queues support a maximum of 3,000 transactions per second with batching (300 without). At 160,000 messages per second the required ingestion rate far exceeds SQS FIFO capacity across any number of queues. SQS also lacks a native model for delivering the same message to four independent consumer teams simultaneously.

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with enhanced fan-out consumers, using game ID as the partition key to guarantee per-shard ordering, with one registered enhanced fan-out consumer per analytics team for dedicated read throughput.
choices.explanation: Kinesis enhanced fan-out delivers a dedicated 2 MB/s per consumer per shard via HTTP/2 server push, eliminating read contention between the four analytics teams. Using game ID as the partition key routes all events for the same game to the same shard, guaranteeing ordered delivery per game. Additional shards can be split to scale ingestion above 1 MB/s write throughput per shard.

choices.text: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) with game-ID-keyed topic partitions, a dedicated consumer group per analytics team, broker auto-scaling policies tied to network throughput metrics, and MSK Connect connectors for downstream service integration.
choices.explanation: Amazon MSK can technically support this workload using topic partitions and consumer groups, but introduces significant operational overhead including broker fleet sizing, storage management, and Kafka configuration expertise. For AWS-native architectures, Kinesis with enhanced fan-out provides equivalent ordering and per-consumer isolation guarantees with a fully managed service and no self-managed infrastructure.

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge Pipes connecting an Amazon DynamoDB Streams source (with game ID as the table partition key) to four downstream Lambda functions - one per analytics team - with reserved concurrency limits isolating each team's processing capacity and DynamoDB TTL discarding records after 24 hours.
choices.explanation: EventBridge Pipes with DynamoDB Streams is designed for change data capture, not high-throughput sensor ingestion. Writing 160,000 messages per second to DynamoDB as a pass-through introduces unnecessary write costs and DynamoDB Streams latency hops. DynamoDB Streams also does not provide the dedicated per-consumer throughput model that Kinesis enhanced fan-out delivers.

questions.tip: Match the requirements - high-volume ingestion with strict ordering and multiple consumers each needing the full stream independently - to the streaming service designed for exactly that access pattern.
questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with enhanced fan-out is purpose-built for high-throughput, ordered, multi-consumer streaming. Enhanced fan-out provides each registered consumer with a dedicated 2 MB/s per shard delivery channel via HTTP/2 push, so all four analytics teams receive the complete stream independently without competing.

**Why it works:** Using game ID as the Kinesis partition key routes all events for a given game to the same shard, preserving in-shard ordering per game. Enhanced fan-out consumers receive their own private delivery channel per shard - four teams reading the same stream do not share or reduce each other's throughput. Shards can be split to scale ingestion capacity horizontally.

**Why the others fail:**
- SQS FIFO: Maximum throughput of 3,000 TPS with batching is orders of magnitude below the required 160,000 messages/second ingestion rate; SQS also cannot deliver the same message to four independent consumer teams.
- Amazon MSK: Functionally capable but requires managing broker fleets, storage, and Kafka configuration. Kinesis achieves the same guarantees as a fully managed AWS-native service.
- EventBridge Pipes with DynamoDB Streams: Designed for change data capture, not sensor ingestion at scale. Introduces unnecessary write costs, additional latency hops, and lacks Kinesis-style dedicated per-consumer throughput.

**Implementation:** Console > Kinesis > Create data stream > Register stream consumers. `aws kinesis register-stream-consumer --stream-arn <arn> --consumer-name analytics-team-1`

questions.question:
The following requirements must be met when configuring a Lambda event source mapping for an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream used for real-time order analytics: process up to 100 records per invocation, discard records older than 60 seconds, buffer incoming records for up to 5 seconds, and begin consuming only records produced after the mapping is created.

Which event source mapping configuration satisfies all four requirements?

choices.text:
{
  "EventSourceArn": "arn:aws:kinesis:us-east-1:123456789012:stream/orders",
  "BatchSize": 100,
  "WindowInSeconds": 5,
  "RecordAgeFilter": 60,
  "StartingPosition": "LATEST"
}
choices.explanation: `WindowInSeconds` and `RecordAgeFilter` are not valid Lambda event source mapping parameters. The correct field names are `MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds` and `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds`. Unrecognized parameter names are silently ignored, leaving both batching window and record age filtering unconfigured.

choices.text:
{
  "EventSourceArn": "arn:aws:kinesis:us-east-1:123456789012:stream/orders",
  "BatchSize": 100,
  "MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds": 5,
  "MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds": 60,
  "StartingPosition": "LATEST"
}
choices.explanation: `MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5` buffers records for up to 5 seconds to build efficient batches up to the `BatchSize` limit. `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds: 60` causes Lambda to automatically skip records older than 60 seconds at the ESM layer before they reach the function. `StartingPosition: LATEST` begins consuming only records produced after the event source mapping is created.

`FilterCriteria` filters records based on pattern matching against event payload data fields, not against internal record metadata such as arrival age. Age-based record discarding is a dedicated Lambda Kinesis ESM capability controlled by the `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds` parameter, not by filter expressions.

choices.text:
{
  "EventSourceArn": "arn:aws:kinesis:us-east-1:123456789012:stream/orders",
  "BatchSize": 100,
  "TumblingWindowInSeconds": 5,
  "MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds": 60,
  "StartingPosition": "TRIM_HORIZON"
}
choices.explanation: `TumblingWindowInSeconds` enables stateful aggregation windows for computing running metrics (such as counts or sums) across fixed time intervals - it does not control the record buffering window used to accumulate batches. `StartingPosition: TRIM_HORIZON` begins processing from the oldest available shard record, causing the function to reprocess all historical stream data rather than only new records.

questions.tip: Review the Lambda event source mapping API reference to identify the correct parameters for controlling batch buffering, age-based record filtering, and stream starting position.
questions.explanation:
Lambda event source mapping for Kinesis provides dedicated parameters for controlling batch collection, age-based record filtering, and stream starting position. These are distinct capabilities with distinct parameter names.

**Why it works:** `MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5` with `BatchSize: 100` instructs Lambda to accumulate records for up to 5 seconds or until 100 records arrive, whichever comes first. `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds: 60` is enforced at the ESM layer - records older than 60 seconds are silently dropped before invocation. `StartingPosition: LATEST` ensures the function processes only records produced after ESM creation.

**Why the others fail:**
- `WindowInSeconds` / `RecordAgeFilter`: These fields do not exist in the Lambda ESM API. The SDK or CLI will reject or silently ignore them, leaving both batch buffering and age filtering unconfigured.
- `FilterCriteria` with age pattern: Lambda filter criteria evaluates JSON field values within the event payload, not internal record metadata like arrival age. `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds` is the correct mechanism for age-based filtering.
- `TumblingWindowInSeconds` / `TRIM_HORIZON`: Tumbling windows are for stateful time-based aggregations (computing results over rolling intervals), not for batching buffer control. `TRIM_HORIZON` starts at the oldest retained shard record, reprocessing all historical stream data.

**Implementation:** `aws lambda create-event-source-mapping --event-source-arn <kinesis-arn> --function-name orders-analytics --batch-size 100 --maximum-batching-window-in-seconds 5 --maximum-record-age-in-seconds 60 --starting-position LATEST`

skills: 2.1.1: Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements.
questions.question:
During a migration from a monolith to microservices on AWS, the checkout service must return a response to the customer immediately after saving a purchase to the database, without waiting for downstream processing. Three downstream services (inventory, shipping, and loyalty) must each independently receive every purchase event and may be unavailable for up to 15 minutes during rolling deployments.

Which TWO AWS services should the solutions architect combine to deliver purchase events durably to all three downstream services?

choices.text: AWS Step Functions - to orchestrate parallel state machine branches that notify each downstream service concurrently, with configurable per-branch retry policies, exponential backoff, and full execution history tracking in CloudWatch Logs.
choices.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates workflows but couples the checkout service to execution completion. Standard Workflows introduce latency waiting for branch results; Express Workflows run asynchronously but do not provide per-service durable message queues that retain events across a 15-minute outage window.

choices.text: Amazon SNS - to publish each purchase event once and simultaneously fan it out to all registered downstream subscribers, fully decoupling the checkout service from the availability and processing rate of each individual downstream service.
choices.explanation: SNS provides the fan-out mechanism. The checkout service publishes to a single SNS topic and SNS delivers the event simultaneously to all subscribers. This decouples the checkout service from the identity, availability, and processing rate of each downstream service.

choices.text: Amazon API Gateway - to expose a single purchase event endpoint that the checkout service calls to trigger all three downstream services through API Gateway HTTP integrations, with Gateway-level throttling and built-in retry on 5xx responses.
choices.explanation: API Gateway provides synchronous HTTP integration, coupling the checkout service response to downstream service availability. A 15-minute deployment window on any downstream service would surface errors through API Gateway back to the checkout service and ultimately to the customer.

choices.text: Amazon SQS - to provide each downstream service with a dedicated, durable message queue that buffers purchase events independently, retaining messages for up to 14 days and enabling automatic reprocessing when services recover after deployment outages.
choices.explanation: A dedicated SQS queue per downstream service provides per-service durability. Messages accumulate during a 15-minute outage and are automatically redelivered when the service recovers. SQS redrive policies route unprocessable messages to a dead-letter queue after a configurable number of receive attempts.

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge event bus with rules targeting a Lambda function per downstream service, using Lambda destination configurations to capture failed invocations and route them to an SQS dead-letter queue after the Lambda retry policy is exhausted.
choices.explanation: EventBridge rules targeting Lambda invoke functions synchronously from EventBridge's perspective, and Lambda async retry behavior covers only short failure windows (2 retries over a few minutes). Without an SQS queue between EventBridge and each Lambda, events produced during a 15-minute outage are not reliably retained and redelivered when the service recovers.

questions.tip: Consider which service publishes a single event to multiple consumers at once, and which service provides a durable per-consumer buffer that outlasts deployment outages.
questions.explanation:
The SNS fan-out to SQS pattern is the canonical AWS design for publishing a single event to multiple independent downstream services with durable per-service buffering. SNS handles simultaneous fan-out delivery; SQS handles per-service durability and automatic retry.

**Why it works:** The checkout service publishes one message to an SNS topic and returns immediately without waiting for downstream processing. SNS simultaneously delivers the message to each subscribed SQS queue. A 15-minute deployment outage on the loyalty service has no effect on the inventory or shipping queues. Messages persist in SQS for up to 14 days and are automatically redelivered when the service recovers, with no custom retry logic required.

**Why the others fail:**
- AWS Step Functions: Provides workflow orchestration but not a durable per-service message buffer. The checkout service remains coupled to orchestration lifecycle, and extended outages are not natively handled by Step Functions as a queuing mechanism.
- Amazon API Gateway: Synchronous HTTP integration means the checkout service blocks for downstream responses. Unavailable services during a deployment window propagate errors back to the customer.
- EventBridge directly to Lambda: Without a dedicated SQS buffer between EventBridge and each Lambda consumer, built-in Lambda async retry windows (typically a few minutes) cannot cover a 15-minute deployment outage.

**Implementation:** Console > SNS > Create topic > Subscribe SQS queues. Configure each SQS queue with a redrive policy pointing to a dead-letter queue for messages that exceed the maximum receive count.

skills: 2.1.1: Designing event-driven, microservice, and/or multi-tier architectures based on requirements.
questions.question:
Migrating a tightly coupled multi-tier web application to an event-driven microservice architecture requires coordinating several steps across Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SQS, and AWS Lambda.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order to complete the migration.

choices.text: Analyze the monolith to identify bounded contexts and define event contracts for all inter-service communication points.
choices.explanation: Domain analysis and event contract definition must precede all technical implementation. Identifying bounded contexts determines which components become independent services and what events flow between them, preventing schema mismatches and expensive redesigns in later phases.

choices.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus and register event schemas in the EventBridge Schema Registry to establish typed event contracts.
choices.explanation: The EventBridge custom event bus and Schema Registry establish shared communication infrastructure and enforce typed contracts before any routing rules or consumer code is written. Registering schemas early allows all teams to generate typed code bindings and ensures services agree on event structure before implementation begins.

choices.text: Configure Amazon EventBridge rules to route events from the custom event bus to dedicated Amazon SQS queues for each target microservice.
choices.explanation: EventBridge routing rules and the SQS queues they target must be created before Lambda event source mappings can reference queue ARNs. Establishing routing infrastructure before consumer code ensures the complete message path exists when Lambda functions are deployed.

choices.text: Deploy each microservice as an AWS Lambda function and configure Lambda event source mappings to connect each function to its corresponding Amazon SQS queue.
choices.explanation: Lambda functions and their SQS event source mappings are deployed after SQS queues exist with stable ARNs. This step completes the event-processing layer by wiring each microservice consumer to its dedicated input queue.

choices.text: Validate end-to-end event flow using Amazon EventBridge event replay and verify correctness through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and Lambda function logs before switching production traffic.
choices.explanation: End-to-end validation using EventBridge event replay is the final step after all infrastructure and application code is in place. Replaying archived events confirms that routing rules, SQS buffers, and Lambda consumers process events correctly before production traffic is switched over.

questions.tip: Follow the dependency chain: event contracts inform schema definitions, routing infrastructure must exist before consumers can be wired, and validation requires the complete pipeline to be in place.
questions.explanation:
Migrating to an event-driven microservice architecture follows a strict dependency order grounded in technical prerequisites. Defining event contracts first ensures all subsequent decisions - schema registry entries, routing rule patterns, Lambda function logic - are grounded in correct domain boundaries. The EventBridge event bus and Schema Registry establish shared infrastructure before routing rules reference specific event patterns. SQS queues must exist with known ARNs before Lambda event source mappings can reference them. Lambda deployment and ESM configuration complete the consumer layer. End-to-end validation with EventBridge event replay confirms correct behavior across the full pipeline before cutting over production traffic.

**Why the others fail:**
- Deploying Lambda functions before SQS queues exist prevents ESM configuration, as the ESM API requires the queue ARN at creation time.
- Creating EventBridge rules before the event bus and schemas are registered risks mismatched event patterns and schema drift across services.
- Running validation before all components are deployed produces incomplete results that cannot confirm full pipeline correctness or catch routing misconfigurations.

**Implementation:** `aws events create-event-bus --name orders-bus` -> `aws schemas create-schema` -> `aws events put-rule --event-bus-name orders-bus` -> `aws lambda create-event-source-mapping --event-source-arn <sqs-arn>` -> `aws events start-replay --event-source-arn <archive-arn>`

skills: 3.1.1: Determining storage services and configurations that meet performance demands.
questions.question:
Block storage for a video transcoding application on Amazon EC2 must deliver consistent 64,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency and persist independently of the instance lifecycle.

Which EBS volume type meets all three requirements?

choices.text: Amazon EBS `gp3` volume provisioned with 64,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s throughput, attached to the EC2 instance as the primary data volume
choices.explanation: `gp3` supports a maximum of 16,000 IOPS per volume regardless of size or provisioned throughput. Requesting 64,000 IOPS exceeds the service limit and is rejected by the API.

choices.text: Amazon EC2 instance store (NVMe SSD) formatted as `ext4` and protected with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager snapshot policies taken every 5 minutes
choices.explanation: EC2 instance store provides very high IOPS but is ephemeral - data is lost when the instance stops, terminates, or hibernates. The requirement for persistence independent of the instance lifecycle rules out instance store, regardless of backup frequency.

choices.text: Amazon EBS `io2` Block Express volume provisioned with 64,000 IOPS, attached to the instance and configured to be retained on instance termination
choices.explanation: `io2` Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MB/s throughput, and sub-millisecond latency per volume. It persists independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle and can be retained after termination by setting `DeleteOnTermination=false`.

choices.text: Amazon FSx for Lustre in Persistent-1 storage deployment mode, mounted on the EC2 instance via the Lustre client for high-throughput access to transcoding assets
choices.explanation: FSx for Lustre is a shared POSIX-compliant parallel file system designed for distributed HPC workloads. It is not per-instance dedicated block storage, does not expose raw block I/O, and cannot be provisioned with a per-instance IOPS guarantee comparable to `io2` Block Express.

questions.tip: Focus on which storage type provides dedicated, consistent IOPS as a block device that outlives the compute instance.
questions.explanation:
`io2` Block Express is the correct choice for workloads requiring both consistent high IOPS and durable block storage independent of instance state.

**Why it works:** `io2` Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s per volume with sub-millisecond latency. EBS volumes persist independently of the EC2 instance and are retained after instance termination when `DeleteOnTermination` is set to `false`.

**Why the others fail:**
- `gp3` provisioned at 64,000 IOPS: `gp3` has a hard maximum of 16,000 IOPS per volume; the API rejects this request.
- EC2 instance store with DLM snapshots: instance store is ephemeral - data is lost on instance stop or termination. Snapshots require a separate EBS volume to restore, violating the direct persistence requirement.
- FSx for Lustre Persistent-1: a shared distributed file system, not dedicated block storage; it cannot provide per-instance provisioned IOPS equivalent to `io2`.

**Implementation:** Console > EC2 > Volumes > Create Volume, select `io2`, set size and IOPS. CLI: `aws ec2 create-volume --volume-type io2 --size <GiB> --iops <IOPS> --availability-zone <AZ>`.

skills: 3.1.1: Determining storage services and configurations that meet performance demands.
questions.question:
Millions of video thumbnails are stored in Amazon S3 under the single key prefix `thumbnails/`. During peak windows the pipeline issues 20,000 GET requests per second against this prefix and observes intermittent 503 SlowDown errors. Thumbnails are generated once and retrieved infrequently by independent workers with low cache-hit potential.

Which change resolves the 503 SlowDown errors?

choices.text: Distribute objects under at least 4 distinct S3 key prefixes (for example, `t0/`, `t1/`, `t2/`, `t3/`) so the 20,000 GET/s load is split across multiple S3 index partitions
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 scales to 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix partition. Distributing 20,000 GET/s across 4 prefixes keeps each partition below 5,000 GET/s, staying within the limit. S3 automatically creates additional partitions as traffic within a prefix grows.

choices.text: Distribute objects under at least 4 distinct S3 key prefixes and simultaneously enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket to further reduce per-request GET latency for pipeline nodes located in remote AWS Regions
choices.explanation: Redistributing across prefixes correctly addresses the partition rate limit. However, S3 Transfer Acceleration routes requests through CloudFront edge locations to reduce geographic latency - it does not raise the per-prefix request rate ceiling and adds unnecessary per-GB cost for same-region EC2 pipeline workers.

choices.text: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin, set `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` headers, and route all pipeline GET requests through the CloudFront domain to offload repeated reads from the S3 origin
choices.explanation: CloudFront caching is effective only when the same objects are requested repeatedly with high cache-hit rates. Because thumbnails are retrieved infrequently by independent workers, cache hit rates will be near zero, leaving the underlying per-prefix partition throttle unsolved for uncached first fetches.

choices.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the thumbnails bucket and configure a lifecycle rule to transition objects not accessed in 30 days to the Infrequent Access tier, reducing S3 GET response latency during peak load windows
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between cost tiers based on access frequency and has no effect on the per-prefix request rate partition limit that causes 503 SlowDown errors. Moving objects to the Infrequent Access tier adds a per-request retrieval fee without addressing request rate throttling.

questions.tip: Identify which specific S3 rate limit is being exceeded, then find the configuration that directly targets that limit.
questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 503 SlowDown errors occur when requests to a single prefix partition exceed 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second. Distributing objects across multiple prefixes splits the load across independent S3 partitions.

**Why it works:** S3 indexes objects by key prefix and partitions the index automatically. Each partition supports up to 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second. Splitting 20,000 GET/s across 4 prefixes keeps each partition below its individual ceiling.

**Why the others fail:**
- Prefix redistribution plus Transfer Acceleration: Transfer Acceleration reduces geographic latency for distant clients but does not raise the per-prefix rate ceiling. It adds cost with no benefit for same-region workers.
- CloudFront with caching: effective for high cache-hit workloads; near-zero hit rates for infrequently accessed one-shot thumbnails leave the partition throttle unsolved.
- S3 Intelligent-Tiering: a storage cost optimization tool that has no effect on request rate limits and may add per-request retrieval fees.

**Implementation:** Re-key objects to use distinct prefix shards. Use `aws s3 cp s3://bucket/thumbnails/file.jpg s3://bucket/t0/file.jpg` (or `t1/`, `t2/`, `t3/` based on a hash of the key) during a migration job.

skills: 3.1.1: Determining storage services and configurations that meet performance demands.
questions.question:
Storage for a high-performance database on Amazon EC2 must be a single 400 GiB EBS volume with consistent 32,000 IOPS and sub-millisecond latency, provisioned using the AWS CLI in `us-east-1a`.

Which command correctly provisions the required volume?

choices.text:
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type gp3 \
  --size 400 \
  --iops 32000 \
  --throughput 1000 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a
choices.explanation: `gp3` volumes support a maximum of 16,000 IOPS per volume, regardless of the `--iops` value specified. Requesting 32,000 IOPS on a `gp3` volume will fail API validation. The `--throughput` flag is valid for `gp3` but cannot compensate for the IOPS ceiling.

choices.text:
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type io1 \
  --size 400 \
  --iops 32000 \
  --multi-attach-enabled \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a
choices.explanation: `io1` enforces a maximum IOPS-to-GiB ratio of 50:1. For a 400 GiB volume, the maximum provisioned IOPS is 20,000 (400 * 50). Requesting 32,000 IOPS exceeds this ratio and the API returns a validation error. `--multi-attach-enabled` is irrelevant to a single-instance database workload.

choices.text:
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type io2 \
  --size 400 \
  --throughput 4000 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a
choices.explanation: The `--throughput` parameter is only valid for `gp3` volume types and is rejected by the API when `--volume-type io2` is specified. To provision IOPS on an `io2` volume the `--iops` flag must be used instead.

choices.text:
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type io2 \
  --size 400 \
  --iops 32000 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a
choices.explanation: `io2` supports a maximum IOPS-to-GiB ratio of 500:1 and an absolute maximum of 256,000 IOPS. For a 400 GiB volume, 32,000 IOPS requires a ratio of 80:1, well within the limit. The `--iops` flag correctly provisions the requested I/O performance.

questions.tip: Review the IOPS limits and the valid CLI parameters for each EBS volume type before selecting.
questions.explanation:
`io2` with `--iops 32000` is the only command that satisfies both the 32,000 IOPS requirement and the 400 GiB volume size constraint.

**Why it works:** `io2` supports up to 500 IOPS per GiB (versus `io1`'s 50:1 limit), so 32,000 IOPS on 400 GiB requires only an 80:1 ratio, which is valid. The `--iops` flag is the correct parameter for provisioning I/O performance on `io2`.

**Why the others fail:**
- `gp3` with `--iops 32000`: `gp3` is capped at 16,000 IOPS regardless of the `--iops` value; the API rejects the request.
- `io1` with `--iops 32000`: `io1` enforces a 50:1 ratio; 400 GiB * 50 = 20,000 max IOPS. The request exceeds this limit.
- `io2` with `--throughput 4000`: `--throughput` is a `gp3`-only parameter; specifying it with `--volume-type io2` causes an API error. `io2` performance is controlled exclusively by `--iops`.

**Implementation:** `aws ec2 create-volume --volume-type io2 --size 400 --iops 32000 --availability-zone us-east-1a`

skills: 3.1.1: Determining storage services and configurations that meet performance demands.
questions.question:
Over the past month, Redshift Spectrum query times against a 200 TB S3 dataset have increased by 60% as the dataset has grown. All files are stored in CSV format under a flat key prefix. S3 data access performance must be improved without reloading data into Redshift managed storage.

Which TWO configurations improve Redshift Spectrum query performance?

choices.text: Convert S3 data files from CSV to Apache Parquet format to enable columnar projection pushdown in Redshift Spectrum, reducing the bytes scanned per query
choices.explanation: Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format. Redshift Spectrum uses projection pushdown to read only the columns required by the query, dramatically reducing the data transferred from S3. This is one of the highest-impact optimizations available for Spectrum query performance.

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the analytics data bucket and update the Redshift Spectrum external schema to reference the accelerate endpoint, reducing network latency for Spectrum leaf node reads from the dataset
choices.explanation: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes requests through CloudFront edge locations to improve upload and download performance for geographically distant clients. Redshift Spectrum compute nodes are co-located in the same AWS region as the S3 bucket and use internal AWS networking, so Transfer Acceleration provides no measurable benefit and adds per-GB cost.

choices.text: Configure the Amazon Redshift cluster for Enhanced VPC Routing so that all Spectrum S3 traffic is routed through the VPC without traversing public internet paths, reducing inter-service latency for large dataset scans
choices.explanation: Enhanced VPC Routing ensures Spectrum S3 traffic flows through the VPC, which improves security posture and enables VPC flow log visibility. It does not materially reduce query execution time because Spectrum nodes already communicate with S3 over the AWS internal network with consistent low latency.

choices.text: Organize S3 objects using Hive-style partition prefixes aligned with common query filter columns (for example, `year=2024/month=01/`) to enable Redshift Spectrum partition pruning for time-range queries
choices.explanation: When the AWS Glue Data Catalog or Redshift external table schema defines partitions matching the S3 prefix structure, Redshift Spectrum skips S3 object listing and data reads for partitions that do not match the query WHERE clause predicates, reducing both S3 API calls and data transferred.

choices.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the analytics bucket with a 30-day monitoring threshold to automatically move infrequently accessed Parquet files to the Infrequent Access tier, reducing storage cost and improving retrieval performance for cold data scans
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage cost by moving objects between access tiers based on frequency. The Infrequent Access tier has the same throughput characteristics as Standard but adds a per-request retrieval fee. It has no effect on Spectrum query scan performance.

questions.tip: Think about what happens to the data before and during a query scan - both data format and data organization affect how much work Spectrum has to do.
questions.explanation:
Converting to Parquet and using Hive-style partitioning are the two highest-impact optimizations for Amazon Redshift Spectrum query performance against S3 data.

**Why they work:** Parquet's columnar layout allows Spectrum to use projection pushdown - reading only relevant columns instead of full rows. Hive-style partitioning enables partition pruning - Spectrum skips S3 objects entirely for partitions that don't match the query filter, reducing both S3 API calls and bytes transferred.

**Why the others fail:**
- S3 Transfer Acceleration: routes through CloudFront edge nodes for geographically distant clients; Spectrum nodes are in the same region as S3 and already use internal AWS fabric. No performance benefit, adds cost.
- Enhanced VPC Routing: improves network security and auditability but does not reduce query execution time since Spectrum already uses internal AWS networking.
- S3 Intelligent-Tiering: a cost optimization tool that moves data between access tiers. The Infrequent Access tier has identical throughput to Standard and adds a per-request retrieval fee.

**Implementation:** Convert CSV to Parquet using AWS Glue ETL: `aws glue create-job --name csv-to-parquet`. Define a partitioned external table in Redshift: `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ... PARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT) STORED AS PARQUET LOCATION 's3://bucket/data/'`.

skills: 3.1.1: Determining storage services and configurations that meet performance demands.
questions.question: Four workloads with distinct performance profiles need to be matched to the appropriate AWS storage service. Match each storage service to the performance characteristic that best describes it.

slots.label: Amazon EFS - Max I/O performance mode

choices.text: Sub-millisecond dedicated block storage providing up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s per volume, designed for latency-sensitive transactional databases running on a single EC2 instance
choices.explanation: `io2` Block Express delivers the highest IOPS and throughput of any EBS volume type with consistent sub-millisecond latency. It provides dedicated block storage to a single EC2 instance, making it ideal for relational databases such as Oracle or SQL Server that require predictable high-frequency random I/O.

choices.text: High-aggregate shared POSIX file system throughput scalable across thousands of EC2 instances simultaneously, with higher per-operation latency compared to single-instance block storage
choices.explanation: EFS Max I/O mode is optimized for highly parallelized workloads (data analytics, media processing, genomics) that need aggregate throughput across many concurrent NFS clients. The trade-off is higher per-operation latency versus General Purpose mode, making it unsuitable for latency-sensitive single-instance applications.

choices.text: Single-digit millisecond object storage purpose-built for latency-sensitive applications, co-located within a specific Availability Zone using isolated storage directories
choices.explanation: S3 Express One Zone delivers up to 10x lower request latency than standard S3 by storing data in a single AZ within purpose-built directory buckets. It is designed for latency-sensitive workloads such as ML training data access, HPC checkpoint storage, and interactive analytics where consistent low-latency object reads are critical.

choices.text: Sub-millisecond POSIX-compliant parallel file system delivering hundreds of GB/s of aggregate throughput, purpose-built for distributed HPC, ML training, and financial simulation workloads
choices.explanation: FSx for Lustre provides a fully managed high-performance parallel file system based on the open-source Lustre filesystem. It integrates natively with S3 and scales to hundreds of GB/s of throughput with sub-millisecond latency, making it ideal for distributed compute workloads requiring a shared high-performance POSIX-compliant file namespace.

questions.tip: Consider both the access pattern (block vs. object vs. file) and whether the workload is single-instance or distributed across many clients.
questions.explanation:
Each storage service is optimized for a distinct performance profile and access pattern.

**io2 Block Express** provides the highest dedicated IOPS per volume with sub-millisecond latency for single-instance block workloads such as transactional databases.

**EFS Max I/O mode** sacrifices per-operation latency in exchange for massive aggregate throughput across thousands of concurrent NFS clients, suited for distributed data processing pipelines.

**S3 Express One Zone** is purpose-built object storage co-located in a single AZ delivering up to 10x lower access latency than standard S3, designed for workloads that need consistent fast object reads without the geographic distribution overhead of standard S3.

**FSx for Lustre** delivers a shared POSIX-compliant parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GB/s aggregate throughput for distributed HPC and ML workloads that require a high-performance shared namespace.

skills: 4.1.1: Designing appropriate storage strategies (for example, batch uploads to Amazon S3 compared with individual uploads).
questions.question:
Individual genomic sequencing files ranging from 1 GB to 8 GB are regularly transferred to an Amazon S3 bucket from on-premises servers across a 500 Mbps internet connection. Network interruptions occur several times per week, causing entire uploads to restart from zero. The solution must minimize wasted data transfer costs and maximize upload resilience.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

choices.text: Use S3 Multipart Upload with a 64 MB part size, retrying only failed parts and uploading multiple parts concurrently
choices.explanation: Multipart Upload splits a large file into independently uploaded parts. Only parts that fail need to be retransmitted, eliminating full-file restarts, and parallel part uploads saturate available bandwidth.

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket and configure the AWS CLI to use the accelerated endpoint, reducing overall upload time and the statistical probability of a network interruption occurring during the transfer
choices.explanation: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront edge locations to reduce latency over long distances, but it provides no part-level checkpoint. A network interruption still requires the entire upload to restart from byte zero.

choices.text: Use AWS DataSync to schedule hourly transfer tasks from the on-premises source to S3, with automatic per-file retry and end-to-end integrity verification using checksums across each sequencing file
choices.explanation: DataSync supports automatic retry and integrity checks but charges $0.0125/GB for data transferred, adding measurable cost on top of standard S3 API pricing. Multipart Upload provides the same part-level resilience without any per-GB transfer fee.

choices.text: Configure an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway on-premises to act as an NFS mount point, then allow the gateway to replicate sequencing files to S3 asynchronously via its background upload process
choices.explanation: Storage Gateway File Gateway is designed for hybrid on-premises file access scenarios, not for high-throughput direct upload optimization. It adds infrastructure management overhead and does not provide finer-grained retry control than Multipart Upload.

questions.tip: Consider which approach gives you the finest granularity of retry and how that affects the amount of data that must be retransmitted after a failure.
questions.explanation:
S3 Multipart Upload is the purpose-built mechanism for large-object transfers. By splitting a file into independently uploaded parts, only failed parts need to be retransmitted after a network interruption, eliminating the cost of restarting the entire upload. Parts are also uploaded in parallel to maximize throughput.

**Why it works:** The file is divided into parts (minimum 5 MB, recommended 64-128 MB each). Each part is uploaded and retried independently. The final object is assembled server-side with `CompleteMultipartUpload`. Already-successful parts are never re-sent.

**Why the others fail:**
- Transfer Acceleration: Improves network path via CloudFront edge nodes but provides no part-level checkpoint; any failure requires restarting the full upload.
- DataSync: Offers file-level retry and integrity checks but adds a $0.0125/GB charge, making it more expensive for pure upload resilience without a scheduling or NFS-migration requirement.
- Storage Gateway File Gateway: Targets hybrid NFS access use cases; adds infrastructure complexity and does not improve part-level retry granularity.

**Implementation:** AWS SDK v2 Transfer Managers (boto3, Java, JavaScript) automatically use Multipart Upload when the object exceeds the configured threshold. Set `multipart_threshold` and `multipart_chunksize` to 64 MB in `~/.aws/config`, or configure the `TransferManager` directly in your application code.

skills: 4.1.1: Designing appropriate storage strategies (for example, batch uploads to Amazon S3 compared with individual uploads).
questions.question:
800 million product image objects are stored in a single Amazon S3 bucket. Cost allocation tags (`department` and `product-line`) must be retroactively applied to all objects within one week. An engineer proposes a multi-threaded application that calls `s3:ListObjectsV2` and `s3:PutObjectTagging` in a loop, but a solutions architect identifies a significantly cheaper and more operationally efficient alternative.

Which solution best minimizes total cost and operational overhead for this tagging task?

choices.text: Create an S3 Inventory configuration to generate a manifest, then submit an AWS Glue ETL job with multiple G.2X worker nodes that calls `PutObjectTagging` in parallel across all listed objects, using Glue job bookmarks to checkpoint progress and resume on failure
choices.explanation: Glue ETL requires DPU worker-hour costs and custom ETL code, and Glue job bookmarks add configuration complexity. This approach is significantly more expensive and operationally heavier than using a purpose-built bulk object operation service.

choices.text: Deploy an Amazon EMR cluster running a Spark application that reads the S3 Inventory manifest, calls `PutObjectTagging` in parallel via the AWS SDK for Java across executors, then auto-terminates the cluster after completion
choices.explanation: EMR Spark can parallelize tagging calls but requires cluster provisioning, EC2 instance-hour costs, and application code development. This overhead is avoidable when a managed, fully serverless bulk tagging service exists for exactly this use case.

choices.text: Create an S3 Inventory configuration to generate a manifest, then submit an S3 Batch Operations job using the `PutObjectTagging` operation with the manifest as input
choices.explanation: S3 Batch Operations is a fully managed, serverless service that processes bulk operations across billions of S3 objects. It charges $0.25 per job plus $1.00 per million object operations, handles retries automatically, generates a completion report, and requires no infrastructure provisioning.

choices.text: Create a Step Functions Express Workflow with a Distributed Map state that iterates over the S3 Inventory manifest in 10,000-object batches, invoking Lambda functions to apply the two tags and publishing completion events to Amazon EventBridge for tracking
choices.explanation: Step Functions Distributed Map with Lambda can achieve high parallelism but incurs Lambda invocation fees, State Transition charges, and EventBridge event costs that compound to a much higher total cost than S3 Batch Operations when applied to 800 million objects.

questions.tip: AWS offers a managed service built specifically for performing bulk operations on millions or billions of S3 objects; consider what infrastructure it eliminates compared to general-purpose compute options.
questions.explanation:
S3 Batch Operations is the purpose-built managed service for bulk object operations at scale. For this tagging task it is the most cost-effective option: a single job definition, an S3 Inventory manifest as input, and a flat rate of $0.25 per job plus $1.00 per million objects with no infrastructure to manage.

**Why it works:** You enable S3 Inventory on the bucket to generate a CSV or ORC manifest, then create a Batch Operations job specifying `PutObjectTagging` and supplying the key-value tag pairs. Batch Operations handles retries, request throttling, IAM permissions, and produces a completion report in S3.

Note that choices starting with "Create an S3 Inventory configuration to generate a manifest, then submit" both use the same correct first step (generating a manifest), but only S3 Batch Operations is purpose-built for this operation -- using Glue ETL requires additional DPU compute costs and custom ETL code.

**Why the others fail:**
- Glue ETL: Requires DPU worker-hour charges and ETL development; significantly higher cost and complexity for a simple metadata update.
- EMR Spark: Cluster provisioning and EC2 instance costs are avoidable for a bulk tagging task.
- Step Functions + Lambda: Lambda invocation fees and State Transition charges make this far more expensive than S3 Batch Operations at 800 million objects.

**Implementation:** Console > S3 > Batch Operations > Create Job > Choose manifest > `PutObjectTagging` operation > Enter tag key-value pairs > Attach IAM role with `s3:PutObjectTagging` > Create.

skills: 4.1.1: Designing appropriate storage strategies (for example, batch uploads to Amazon S3 compared with individual uploads).
questions.question:
A local directory containing 10,000 mixed-size files must be uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket from an EC2 instance. The upload must skip `.tmp` files, apply AWS KMS server-side encryption, and only transfer files that do not already exist in the destination or have been modified since the last run.

Which AWS CLI command correctly satisfies all three requirements?

choices.text:
aws s3 cp /data/files s3://my-bucket/uploads/ \
  --recursive \
  --exclude "*.tmp" \
  --sse aws:kms
choices.explanation: `aws s3 cp --recursive` copies all matching source files unconditionally without comparing them against the destination. It does not skip already-uploaded or unchanged files, violating the incremental-transfer requirement.

choices.text:
aws s3 sync /data/files s3://my-bucket/uploads/ \
  --exclude "*.tmp" \
  --sse aws:kms
choices.explanation: `aws s3 sync` compares source and destination by size and last-modified timestamp, transferring only new or modified files. `--exclude "*.tmp"` skips temporary files, and `--sse aws:kms` applies KMS server-side encryption to each uploaded object.

choices.text:
aws s3 sync /data/files s3://my-bucket/uploads/ \
  --delete \
  --exclude "*.tmp" \
  --sse aws:kms
choices.explanation: The `--delete` flag removes objects from the S3 destination that no longer exist in the local source directory. This behavior was not requested and could cause unintended data loss in the S3 bucket.

choices.text:
aws s3 sync /data/files s3://my-bucket/uploads/ \
  --exclude "*.tmp" \
  --server-side-encryption aws:kms
choices.explanation: `--server-side-encryption` is not a valid parameter for `aws s3 sync`. The correct flag is `--sse`. This command fails with an `Unknown options: --server-side-encryption` error.

questions.tip: Identify which command subcommand performs built-in source-to-destination comparison to skip unchanged files, then verify the exact flag names accepted by that subcommand.
questions.explanation:
`aws s3 sync` is the correct command for incremental directory uploads. It compares the source directory against the S3 destination and transfers only objects that are new or have changed (by size and last-modified date). Combined with `--exclude "*.tmp"` and `--sse aws:kms`, all three requirements are met.

**Why it works:** `sync` builds an inventory of source objects, compares them to the destination listing, and uploads only the differences. `--exclude` patterns use shell glob syntax applied before the comparison. `--sse aws:kms` sets the `x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms` header on each `PutObject` request.

**Why the others fail:**
- `cp --recursive`: Copies every matching source file regardless of whether an identical object already exists at the destination; no incremental logic.
- `sync --delete`: Adds deletion of S3 objects absent from the source, which was not requested and introduces data-loss risk.
- `sync --server-side-encryption`: Invalid flag name; `--sse` is the correct parameter; the command exits with an unknown-option error.

**Implementation:** Run from any host with the AWS CLI installed and IAM permissions for `s3:PutObject`, `s3:ListBucket`, and `kms:GenerateDataKey` on the target bucket and KMS key.

skills: 4.1.1: Designing appropriate storage strategies (for example, batch uploads to Amazon S3 compared with individual uploads).
questions.question:
Over six months, hundreds of thousands of incomplete multipart uploads have accumulated in an S3 bucket, occupying tens of terabytes and generating ongoing storage charges. The root cause is a batch pipeline that initiates multipart uploads for large compressed archives and frequently fails mid-upload without cleanup. Both the existing backlog and future accumulation must be addressed.

Which TWO actions together resolve both the existing and future incomplete multipart upload costs?

choices.text: Add an S3 lifecycle rule with the `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` action set to expire incomplete parts after 7 days
choices.explanation: The `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle action aborts incomplete multipart uploads and deletes all associated parts once they exceed the configured age. It applies retroactively to existing accumulated parts and prevents future parts from persisting indefinitely.

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent object versions after 1 day, which also purges incomplete multipart upload parts from storage billing
choices.explanation: Versioning and noncurrent-version expiration apply only to versioned S3 objects. Incomplete multipart upload parts are tracked separately from objects and are completely unaffected by noncurrent-version lifecycle rules.

choices.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket so that incomplete multipart upload parts are automatically transitioned to the Archive Access tier after 90 days, reducing their ongoing storage cost to near zero
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering transitions complete objects between access tiers based on access patterns. Incomplete multipart upload parts are not complete objects and are not eligible for Intelligent-Tiering transitions; they continue to be billed at standard storage rates.

choices.text: Update the upload application to explicitly call `s3:AbortMultipartUpload` in the exception handling block whenever a multipart upload fails or is cancelled before completion
choices.explanation: Calling `AbortMultipartUpload` in the application error path immediately deletes all already-uploaded parts for a failed upload, preventing future incomplete-part accumulation in real time rather than waiting for a lifecycle rule window to expire.

choices.text: Create an S3 Event Notification that invokes a Lambda function on `s3:ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload` events to identify and abort any orphaned upload IDs and delete their associated parts
choices.explanation: `s3:ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload` fires only when a multipart upload is successfully completed, not when one is abandoned or fails mid-upload. No event is emitted for orphaned incomplete uploads, so this Lambda would never trigger for the cleanup use case.

questions.tip: Consider two independent layers of defense: one at the infrastructure level that enforces an age limit on incomplete parts, and one in the application that cleans up immediately on failure.
questions.explanation:
The most complete solution combines two complementary actions that address both the existing backlog and future accumulation.

**Why they work:**
- `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle rule: retroactively expires existing accumulated parts older than the configured number of days AND enforces an upper-bound age on any future incomplete uploads -- all without application code changes.
- Application-level `AbortMultipartUpload`: immediately frees storage for each failed upload in real time, reducing the window during which charges accumulate to near zero rather than up to 7 days.

**Why the others fail:**
- Versioning + noncurrent expiration: Targets versioned objects only; incomplete parts are not objects and are unaffected by this lifecycle action.
- Intelligent-Tiering: Transitions complete objects between access tiers; incomplete parts cannot be tiered.
- Event Notification on `CompleteMultipartUpload`: Only fires on successful completions; orphaned parts generate no completion event and are invisible to this trigger.

**Implementation:** Console > S3 > Bucket > Management > Lifecycle rules > Create rule > Apply to all objects > `Abort incomplete multipart uploads` > Set days to 7. In the application, capture the `UploadId` returned by `CreateMultipartUpload` and call `AbortMultipartUpload` with it in every catch or finally block that handles upload failure.
